b: Last night Abdelrahman ElGendy, writer and former political prisoner in Egypt, won the National Book Award in Nonfiction for his book Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming. It’s one of literature’s highest honors and a major achievement for a writer, but ElGendy couldn’t be there to accept his award, as he was denied a visa to enter the US.

But it’s not the only indignity he’s suffered around his win. A day before the award ceremony, The New York Times ran a story questioning his eligibility for a National Book Award, based in part on details in a New Yorker piece by ElGendy and the National Book Foundation’s own written requirements. The National Book Foundation (which administers the National Book Awards), ElGendy’s publishers, and fellow nominees all defended him to The Times. But even in covering ElGendy’s win, The Times cited themselves to continue to raise doubts about his eligibility.

The National Book Foundation has been clear about their process around ElGendy’s nomination, and responded to the initial Times story to clarify their decision and their vetting of ElGendy’s eligibility in a statement, which is available in full on their website. The main point of the statement is that in 2024, the NBF expanded their eligibility requirements “in an effort to create a more robust celebration of literature published in the United States.” The goal, as I read it, was for the Awards to reflect American books as widely as possible and at every stage of their process:

We are proud of this decision, and the opportunity to accept submissions from the widest possible array of voices shaping today’s canon of American literature, and to recognize the exceptional books that make up each year’s Longlists, Finalists, and Winners.

This is an acknowledgment that American literature has always been written from many backgrounds—a ground-breaking and best-selling book like 1845’s Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass was written by someone whose citizenship and humanity were in technical, legal doubt, but no one would question its central place in the American canon. The NBF’s expanded criteria acknowledges that where someone’s rent money or taxes go is not necessarily reflective of their ability to write something important for an American publisher. The NBF’s goal is to celebrate American letters in their full breadth, and their decision to bend their own rules reflects this intention.

The choice is also a reading of ElGendy’s own intentions—he didn’t leave the US on a lark. It was an agonizing and fearful decision, according to his New Yorker essay, and a part of his longer struggle for stability and safety. An unsafe political environment full of ICE raids and a crackdown on pro-Palestinian protesters drove him away:

One day, I caught myself wondering what I wanted to be wearing when ICE came to my door. At that moment, I recognized the logic of the system that I had fled to the U.S. to escape—one in which speaking and writing openly made you a target and the possibility of imprisonment reorganized the smallest routines of daily life.
I knew then that I had to uproot my life again. I left the U.S. in late April and resettled in Europe, entering what I hoped would be a temporary exile within my exile.

The decision to maintain his eligibility seems to have come down to an acknowledgment of ElGendy’s unique situation in Trump’s America and the NBF’s broader values and goals, as opposed to the letter of their own law. ElGendy’s eligibility for a National Book Award is a reflection of the quality of his writing and the fact that his book is an important part of contemporary American literature, which trumps any technicalities about where he has a lease.

Because Huna is a triumph, a beautiful book. It’s a testament to writing as an essential tool for life. In a piece in our pages called “The Thick Muddy Soil of Language: On Mosab Abu Toha’s Forest of Noise,” ElGendy celebrated writing’s power to meet this moment: “Together, the poems in Forest of Noise emerge as a potent invocation, an act of writing not only about survival, but as survival.”

And in an essay about the process of crafting his memoir, ElGendy writes of choosing to write in English, and of how he decided to organize Huna “in the form of an ‘anbara, an old Egyptian prison call-and-response tradition through which prisoners speak across cells, answering one another through the naddara, the small meshed opening in a cell door.” (There’s also more in an interview with Samaa Khullar and in another short, NBA Finalists’ interview, where I was happy to read that ElGendy’s a procrastinator too.)
ElGendy is a great writer, and an important new voice. Huna is a deserving winner of this major award, and the celebration doesn’t deserve to be marred by more ugly second-guessing of his status.
